newsitem.title: UK: BP says 1996 "exceptional" for oil demand and price.
newsitem.headline: BP says 1996 "exceptional" for oil demand and price.

text.p: Last year's sharp rise in oil prices was the result of unusually cold weather and low inventories, rather than a sign that prices were entering a new higher range, the chief economist of British Petroleum Co Plc said on Wednesday.
"1996 was an exceptional year rather than the start of a new high price oil era," Peter Davies said at the launch of the BP Statistical Review of World Energy 1997.
World Benchmark Brent blend crude climbed to a six-year high of just over $25 a barrel in October last year, but has since slumped to less than $18.
He said oil prices appeared to have settled back into their 10-year trading range between $15 and $20.
According to BP's review, oil consumption world-wide rose by 2.4 percent in 1996 to 69.55 million barrels per day (bpd).
Outside the former Soviet Union consumption grew by 3.3 percent in 1996, well above the average seen for the last 10 years, and double the growth seen in 1995.
The increase was caused largely by strong demand in North America and Europe, helped by a 1995/96 winter that was both colder and longer than average.
The situation was aggravated as refiners, especially in the U.S., decided to keep low stocks in order to cut costs, Davies said.
"Commercial oil inventories were at record lows entering 1996 and were further weakened in early 1996 by the very cold weather and extended winter in the Northern hemisphere," he said.
In addition, global economic growth was above-trend, although this was outstripped by oil demand.

Nevertheless, world oil output still outpaced demand last year, growing by 2.9 percent to 69.69 million bpd with the expansion of production in all regions and the re-entry of Iraq to the market in December topping up volumes, the review said.
"The underlying tendency of supply to drive the market gradually took charge. Prices have reverted to the last 10 years' trading range of $15-$20," said Davies.
The review showed a two percent increase in proved reserves last year to 1037 billion barrels.
"The dominant theme of the last decade is the realisation that supply is not a problem," said Davies.
